demos.objective: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
demos.slide: syn-s01: slide 1 of 7; slide 1 of 3 in seg-01
demos.chunks:
[syn-s01-c1] (syn-s01) Lecture 3 | Organizing Data and Object Basics | Sample Course 101
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script: We organize things every day to make them easier to use. Think of a music playlist—you put songs in a certain order so you can find and play them quickly. When people line up at a bus stop, they get on in the order they arrived, so everyone knows who goes next. Even the undo button in a program works the same way—it removes the most recent change first, just like taking the last thing you added off a stack. All of these are ways to keep information or actions neat and predictable.

[syn-s02-c1] (syn-s02) Outline | - Organizing data | - Object basics
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script: Let’s start with something we all do every day—organizing things to make them easier to use. Think of a music playlist. You put songs in a certain order so you can find and play them quickly. Or picture people waiting at a bus stop. They get on the bus in the same order they arrived, so everyone knows who’s next. Even the undo button in a text editor works this way—it removes the most recent change first, like peeling off the top layer of a stack. These are all simple ways we arrange data so it’s ready when we need it.

demos.question: Which collection does not allow duplicate items?
demos.options:
A: Bag
B: Set
C: List
D: Stack
demos.misconception: Bag rejects duplicates: Believes a bag keeps only one copy of each item.
demos.chunks:
[syn-s05-c1] (syn-s05) Collections | - Bag | - Set | - List | - Stack | - Queue | - Map
[syn-p03-c2] (reference) A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.
demos.title: Bags allow duplicates, sets don’t
demos.text: A lot of you picked bag, thinking it rejects duplicates. But the lesson says a bag is like a shopping bag—you can toss in two identical apples and both stay. A set is the one that acts like a club guest list: if your name is already on it, you don’t get in again. So the collection that does not allow duplicates is the set.
